newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU parliament gives Commission new BSE warning.
newsitem.headline: EU parliament gives Commission new BSE warning.

text.p: More than 100 Euro MPs on Thursday backed a censure motion which would have forced European Commission President Jacques Santer and his 19 commissioners out of office for mishandling the mad cow crisis.

But the censure motion tabled by Belgian Socialist Jose Happart was blocked by 326 members of the assembly, falling far short of the two-thirds of votes cast and an absolute majority of 314 votes it needed to be passed.
"The motion was convincingly rejected. I am very pleased," a relieved Santer told a news conference after the vote.
He agreed reforms were necessary but regretted that the Commission was having to work under threat of sanctions.

On Wednesday, the EU assembly voted overwhelmingly for a resolution presented by the mainstream Socialist and Christian Democrat groups giving Santer nine months to put matters right or face another censure motion which they would back.
Between them they have more than enough votes to force it through.

Reform would not be easy, Santer said, noting that pressure was already being applied not to alter the costly Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) even though the EU's planned expansion eastwards and financial constraints made change essential.

EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler told the same conference he had for years been promoting measures to improve food quality and to protect the environment and counted on support from the directly elected assembly.
The Commission last week agreed to reorganise its food safety services to put the popular and energetic consumer affairs chief, Italian Emma Bonino, in overall control.
Bonino will also run a new veterinary inspection office, formerly managed by the powerful agricultural directorate.
Asked whether she had the resources to meet the challenges, Bonino told the news conference that extra funds for more staff were due to be provided by the end of April.
"The budget will be the moment of truth," she said.
Happart's censure motion was the fourth since the European Parliament was first elected in 1979 and attracted 118 votes -- the most so far.

But he was nevertheless disappointed. "I regret that a majority in the European Parliament refused to sanction the Commission and the British government for serious past faults," he said in a statement.

He said his first thoughts were for the victims of mad cow disease - bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) -- which has been linked with a new version of the human brain-wasting disease Creutzfeld Jakob Disease.
He told Reuters later he had promised to help the families of victims of BSE to sue the Commission and the British government.

Happart, who found support from across the political spectrum, said the Commission had failed to give priority to the protection of public health and had caved in under British pressure to ease control measures.
French Socialist Andre Laignel, a supporter of the motion, said that despite pressure from national governments, including Paris, Euro MPs had shown their independence.
"It's a serious warning to Santer," he told reporters.
Most socialists voted against the motion saying it was "ill-judged".
"But the Commission will have to face a much more serious threat of censure in the coming months," Socialist Group leader, Pauline Green, said in a statement.

On Wednesday, the parliament endorsed a highly critical report by a special committee of inquiry into the crisis caused by the public health scare which followed the announcement last March that BSE could be transmitted to humans.
The report by a 19-member cross-party committee condemned Britain's failure to enforce BSE controls and the refusal of its Minister of Agriculture to appear before the inquiry.
But the parliament, which has no power to take action against member states, shied away from demanding that the Commission take legal action against Britain.
Santer said the Commission had discretionary powers and that it would study all the facts before considering possible proceedings.
